label: Gluing Constructions
notes: Open by framing the chapter's central tension: gluing CAT(k) pieces along the wrong seam destroys curvature, while gluing along the right seam preserves it. Reshetnyak's theorem names the right seam precisely. Promise the audience a runnable mental model where each picture is tied to a comparison inequality they can check.

label: What Gluing Means
notes: Define the gluing of two spaces along an isometry of chosen subspaces, with the induced quotient pseudometric measuring shortest concatenated paths that may cross the seam. Stress that the seam is identified pointwise, so a path can re-enter either piece. The whole chapter studies which seams keep the result a length space of bounded curvature.

label: Convex Subspaces
notes: Recall that a subset is convex when every geodesic between its points stays inside it, and complete when it is closed as a metric space. These two adjectives are the hypotheses Reshetnyak demands of the seam. Give the half-plane boundary line and a metric ball as contrasting examples so learners feel why convexity is restrictive.

label: Reshetnyak's Gluing Theorem
notes: State the headline result: gluing two CAT(k) spaces along a complete isometric convex subspace yields a CAT(k) space, for k at most zero. Emphasize that convexity of the seam is exactly what lets a comparison triangle straddling the seam be rebuilt in the model plane without increasing distances. This is the engine for every construction that follows.

label: Why Convexity of the Seam
notes: Walk through the proof idea: a geodesic triangle crossing the seam decomposes at the convex wall, and convexity guarantees the crossing point lies on a geodesic of the wall. Reassembling the comparison triangles hinge-side by hinge-side keeps the configuration thin. Without convexity the crossing geodesic can shortcut outside the wall and fatten the triangle.

label: Thinness Across the Seam
notes: Use the diagram to make the comparison test concrete: a triangle with one vertex in each piece crosses the seam, and the corresponding comparison triangle in the model plane is at least as fat. Distances measured to the comparison points dominate the real ones, so the glued triangle inherits the CAT(k) thinness condition exactly.

label: Gluing Along a Point
notes: Specialize the seam to a single point, which is trivially complete convex. The wedge of two CAT(0) spaces at a point is again CAT(0); this is how bouquets and wedges of trees or disks acquire non-positive curvature. Note the geodesic between points in different petals must pass through the wedge point, a useful sanity check.

label: Gluing Along a Geodesic
notes: Take the seam to be a complete geodesic line or segment, which is convex. Gluing two CAT(0) half-planes along their boundary line rebuilds the plane; gluing three along a shared line gives a book of pages, a branched flat space that is still CAT(0). The branch locus is where several convex walls coincide.

label: The Doubling Construction
notes: Double a CAT(0) space across a complete convex subset by gluing two copies along that subset using the identity. Reshetnyak guarantees the double is CAT(0), and the swap symmetry fixes the seam. Mention that doubling a convex region of the plane across its boundary produces a Riemannian-flat object with a curvature singularity only where convexity could fail.

label: Trees and Graphs of Spaces
notes: Iterate gluing along convex walls following a tree or graph pattern: vertex spaces are CAT(0) blocks, edge spaces are the convex walls they share. A tree of spaces stays CAT(0) by repeated Reshetnyak; a graph of spaces with cycles needs link conditions instead. This is the structural backbone of many non-positively curved complexes.

label: When the Seam Is Not Convex
notes: Show the failure mode: gluing along a non-convex subset lets a shortest path kink incorrectly at the seam, creating a geodesic bigon or a fat comparison triangle. The curvature bound breaks locally near the kink. This is the negative control in the notebook lab and explains why both hypotheses on the seam are indispensable.

label: Recap and Examples
notes: Recap the logic chain: convex complete seam, then Reshetnyak, then CAT(k) is preserved, then wedges, doubles, books, and trees of spaces follow as corollaries. Leave learners with the inspection habit from the notebook: name the points, identify the convex wall, and verify thinness on a triangle that straddles the seam before trusting the construction.
